title: Pediatric Burn Management
keywords: Lund-Browder head starts at 19 percent in infants versus 7 in adults
add maintenance fluid on top of resuscitation fluid — kids can't do this without it, low glycogen reserve
burn center referral over 10 percent TBSA or any critical area regardless of size
all significant peds burns get an accidental-vs-non-accidental trauma screen

ageRange: Birth through adolescence — the Lund-Browder table below is specifically what makes this tool age-sensitive where the adult rule of nines is not
purpose: The pediatric-specific parts of burn management that the adult-oriented parkland-formula card doesn't cover: accurate %TBSA estimation in a child (the rule of nines is wrong for kids), the maintenance-fluid addition kids need that adults don't, and burn-center referral thresholds.

body.text: Why the adult rule of nines doesn't work in children

A young child's head is proportionally much larger, and their legs proportionally much smaller, than an adult's — using the adult rule of nines on a toddler overestimates leg burns and badly underestimates head/scalp burns. The Lund-Browder chart corrects for this by scaling the head and leg percentages with age.

All other regions (trunk, arms, neck, genitalia) are essentially constant across ages in the Lund-Browder chart and match the standard rule-of-nines figures — it's specifically the head and legs that shift with growth. Use the nearest age band; interpolate if the child's age falls between two rows.
Fluid resuscitation — the same formula PLUS something adults don't need

The resuscitation-volume math itself (4 mL/kg/%TBSA lactated Ringer's, half over the first 8 hours, rest over 16 — see the parkland-formula card) is the same formula at any age. What's missing if you stop there in a child: kids have low glycogen reserves and can become hypoglycemic during burn resuscitation if given ONLY resuscitation fluid with no dextrose-containing maintenance fluid running alongside it. A plain adult-style Parkland calculation, run in isolation, under-resuscitates a child's actual fluid needs.

items: Add weight-based maintenance fluid (Holliday-Segar: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg + 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg + 1 mL/kg/h for each kg above 20) running separately alongside the resuscitation fluid — this maintenance fluid is typically dextrose-containing (e.g. D5 in a dilute saline solution) specifically to cover the hypoglycemia risk, while the resuscitation fluid itself stays lactated Ringer's without dextrose.

The Galveston formula is an alternative, body-surface-area-based approach purpose-built for pediatric burns that bundles resuscitation and maintenance into one calculation (5000 mL × %TBSA × BSA[m²] + 2000 mL × BSA[m²] for the first 24 hours) — some pediatric burn centers prefer it over a Parkland-plus-maintenance approach; know which convention your receiving burn center uses if transferring.

Titrate to urine output of 1 mL/kg/h in children under 30 kg (vs. 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults) — already noted on the parkland-formula card, restated here because it's easy to under-shoot if defaulting to the adult target out of habit.

body.text: Burn center referral — lower threshold in children

items: Partial-thickness or deeper burns > 10% TBSA (vs. the general adult threshold, which is similar but children tolerate a given %TBSA worse than adults of the same nominal burn size).
ANY burn — regardless of %TBSA — involving the face, hands, feet, genitalia/perineum, or major joints, or any full-thickness (3rd degree) burn at any size.
Circumferential burns (extremity or torso) — risk of compartment syndrome/restrictive ventilation as edema develops; escharotomy may become necessary.

A notably LOWER bar for referral consideration in young children even below the 10% threshold — pain control, frequent dressing changes, and family/caregiver support needs alone are often enough reason in a young child, independent of burn severity.

body.text: Every pediatric burn evaluation includes a screen for non-accidental trauma — pattern (stocking/glove distribution, clear immersion lines, symmetric/bilateral burns, sharply demarcated borders), a history inconsistent with the child's developmental stage or the injury pattern, and delayed presentation are all red flags. This is a routine part of the workup, not an accusation reserved for suspicious-looking cases.
